subject: Council Hearing on Zoning Consolidation on July 1
comment: I want to respectfully request that the City Council postpone the scheduled hearing and possible action on the massive Mixed Use Zoning Consolidation for the following reasons: 1. The July 1 hearing date takes place during a major holiday week, when many people who would like to participate will be out of town. 2. The over 1900 page Staff Report was released on Friday, June 27. It is manifestly unfair to expect interested citizens less than 4 full days to go through the over 1400 pages of the Staff Report that pertains to the Zoning Consolidation. That is the equivalent of 3 500 page very technical coding volumes that City personnel have been working on for many months. 3. While certain parts of the Zoning Consolidation have been previously available, changes have been both made and proposed. Teasing these out and evaluating their consequences requires more time than the less than 4 days provided. 4. The scheduling of the hearing and possible action date so soon after release of the Staff Report and during a holiday week, gives the misleading impression that action on such a consequential change to City Zoning is being done during a time frame to ensure as little citizen participation as possible. I am POSITIVE that this is NOT the case. However, I have already heard this opinion ( in language not fit for publication ) from people who follow Council actions. Please do not let the Zoning Consolidation carry this burden. Once again, please do the sensible thing and postpone the hearing and possible action. Not generated by AI.

subject: Sugar House Business District Zoning
comment: To The City Council: I'm writing in regard to the proposed zoning change for the Sugar House Business District. My understanding is that, if the change is approved, buildings up to 165 feet in height would be allowed in the district. However, buildings of this scale would have a significant detrimental impact on the character of the district which could substantially impact economic activity in the district. The general height of buildings in the Sugar House Business District is firmly established—not only by existing ordinance but, more to the point, by the buildings in the district that collectively establish a visual coherence. Even with extensive new construction over the past ten years or so, the district has retained much of its essential sense of place—to a great extent because of this visual coherence that reinforces it. A distinct character or identity—a distinct sense of place—has been demonstrated in commercial districts across the country to be the foundation of a vibrant economy. Allowing for significantly taller buildings (150 feet or taller) risks compromising the district identity of the Sugar House Business District and in turn negatively impacting the district's economy. I strongly encourage you to endorse the alternative forwarded by the Sugar House Community Council that proposes to limit building height to no more than 110 feet on the north side of 2100 South between 700 East and 1300 East and to approximately 50 feet along the east side of Highland Drive between 2100 South and I-80. Doing so would reinforce the existing scale of the business district. The eastern portion of the latter block—closer to 1300 East—could still accommodate taller buildings if certain community benefits, such as a meaningful percentage of affordable housing, are incorporated. Thank you for your attention. Bim Oliver

subject: Comment - MU Zoning Consolidation PLNPCM2024-00707
comment: Dear SLC Council Members – For your consideration of adopting the ordinance to rezone existing zoning districts to Mixed Use zoning districts, I am asking you to please support a transition period of a minimum of 3 months (preference up to 6 months) to allow developers to utilize the current zone standards for projects actively in the design process. Our organization currently has a parcel of land under contract in the North Temple district of the city and has invested time and money into a design an affordable housing complex with a building form that meets the current zoning standards. The feasibility of the project is dependent on the current zoning and would be subject to a significant setback due to timing and redesign efforts with the new zone standards, negatively impacting the project progress thus far. As an affordable housing developer of family sized rental units, there are already significant hurdles to make these projects pencil. This change in zones would compromise the project from being implemented. Thank you for your consideration and understanding of these affordable housing challenges. West Side Proud! -Todd J. comment: Below are some thoughts on the MU zoning consolidation, some with reference to the "Meeting Materials" PDF released Friday (6/27). > I don't know if this is helpful but is it possible the Council could approve this in stages?. On July 1 they could approve committing to the consolidation and what the standards in each MU zone are (setbacks and parking and windows and whatnot) and set an effective date 6 months away. They could continue to get input on the map----on what properties should be in what zone----and approve that at some future meeting up to, say, 3 months away. This might be helpful if a lot of the public concern is not regarding the rules within a zone but regarding which properties are placed in which zone. Or maybe you can't realistically do that, because of how the draft ordinance is structured. But the Council could pass it all on July 1, still with an effective date 6 or more months away, and just know that they expect the option to revise the maps up until the last 3 months of the transition period. > I think the public interest would be served if the Midas and Snelgrove blocks are zoned at MU-5 or 6, not at MU-8. This was mentioned as Item 6 in the Planning Division memo of June 4. As noted in the memo, this approach will allow time and leverage to strategize ways to make the area remain conducive to occupancy by locally owned businesses. > I think the stepback requirements for MU-8 and MU-11 should be set at 10' stepback no higher than 45' if the right-of-way is narrower than 90', and at 10' stepback no higher than 85' otherwise. Right now they're houses, and I'm assuming under MU-2 they could stay houses. But in my opinion the road infrastructure and overall context is such that MU-2 sized businesses could develop there in the future and it would be fine.... like 15th/15th or Stratford/Glenmare or 900S between 200-500E. (I am assuming that I'm interpreting things correctly and that a single-family home can sit on a MU-* property and be a conforming use. And further, I'm assuming that the zoning change doesn't cause harm to a current resident/owner who want their house to continue to just be a house.) I might have the same opinion about other areas too. For example, it is weird to me that the west side of Redwood Road between 600-800S (Indiana) is MU-5 but the houses on the east side that directly abut Redwood couldn't be MU-2. I recognize that the scope of this consolidation maybe did not include looking at any current residential-zoned properties, and if that's the case then this would be a consideration maybe for another time? > I think the interior of Brickyard can max out its MU. Right now it is just MU-5. > I think these Upper Avenues properties could be MU-6: 6th Ave / E Street (Smith's); 8th Ave / D Street And these could be MU-3 6th Ave / G Street 9th Ave / K Street There's already apartment or condo buildings in the Avenues that are 5 or 6 or more stories tall (IIRC the Pollyana at 1st / F, and the Northridge Heights on 5th between G and H). > Looking at the draft zoning text amendments, V3. Technically it doesn't say that outdoor midblock walkways have to be open to the public ... shouldn't it? It sets no standards for "open to the public"... subject: 128 N Street Zoning change request, PLNPCM2024-01079
comment: Comments to the Salt Lake City Council regarding 128 N Street Zoning change request, PLNPCM2024-01079 1 July 2025 As the chair of the Greater Avenues Community Council Land Use Committee, I can report to the Council that the Committee had no substantive objections to this project as originally proposed. Unfortunately, the process by which this project was approved rendered that position almost immediately irrelevant. When I and others attended the Planning Commission hearing to make comments we found a proposal had been changed both in design scope and in the requested Zone change, reportedly within days of the Hearing. So recently in fact, that an updated site plan was not available to the Commission. This effectively removed the ability of the Land Use Committee to make informed public comment on the project. I suspect that a better project might have resulted from early public input on the actual project design, and I submit that the combination of new scale of construction and a new requested Zone result in an essentially new project, which should trigger a continuance for additional public comment period. I also commented to the Planning Commission that the assertion that no tenants will be displaced by this project is open to interpretation: Planning Staff reported garages to be demolished as previously included with the rental of the original building's units. Therefore tenants that depend on secure garage storage will be displaced. Lastly , the City Council has wisely required that a public benefit should be present with a change in zoning. The original listed public benefit project was disallow as already required. The new public benefit of this project was providing family housing, and this was tacitly accepted by the Planning Commission when it voted to approve. I submit that the construction of market rate two bedroom apartments does not increase family housing, and I request that the Council consider providing further clarification on the scope of required public benefit. Respectfully Submitted, Jim Jenkin

subject: MU Zoning Consolidation
comment: Comments on Mixed Use Zoning Consolidation Dear Council Members, The preamble to Zoning consolidation efforts in Salt Lake City always talks about preserving the character of the neighborhood, yet these proposals contain a provision that has the potential to alter the character of neighborhoods considerably, and that is the restriction of additional setback and step-back protections in Historic areas to City Register sites and direct Zone borders. I don't believe this has ever been done before and I question whether it is consistent with Department of the Interior guidance on Historic Districts. Simply stated, the Character of a historic neighborhood is defined by the contributory structures within it, not by those few that owners have chosen to list on the Register. A block face may have a corner historic building on both ends, but only one may be on the register. Thus the other can be encroached upon and the character of the block/face lost. I urge the Council to require that setback and step-back protections be considered whenever construction abuts contributory historic structures. Jim Jenkin

subject: Mountain Bike Trails
comment: Hi, I live in Salt Lake City and frequent many foothill trails in SLC. I hike and bike the trails 2-3x a week. And we need more mountain bike trails. What happened to the approved trail expansion a few years ago that was passed? Many smaller towns across the west like Hailey, ID, Boise, ID, towns in OR, towns in CO have been expanding their mountain bike trail systems every year. Towns like Fruita, CO economy was saved by mountain biking. Every year I visit surrounding towns and they seem to be adding new mountain bike trails uphill and downhill directional trails. Can we please add more mountain bike trails? Many trails could be linked from Black Mountain to Emmigration canyon, like via Miners Trail or other deer trails that people recreate on. The backside of Lost Lad trail could be linked to Bountiful more easily, and expanded past the Towers. Trails at the top of Ensign peak could be expanded. Mount Van Cott could be linked to the mountain bike trails up by twin peaks and Terror Ridge. We could link mountain bike trails to Park City very easily. I know several Mountain Bikers that try to ride on dirt all the way to Park City and it's impossible. Think Big! The people of Salt Lake need more mountain bike trails. Thank you! -Chelsea McGowan

subject: Support for Mixed-Use Zoning Consolidation
comment: Dear Mayor Mendenhall and City Council Members, Salt Lake County Neighbors for More Neighbors strongly supports the proposed Mixed-Use Zoning Consolidation (PLNPCM2024-00707). This important reform will make Salt Lake City's zoning code simpler, clearer, and better aligned with Salt Lake City's values and vision for a more affordable, walkable, and inclusive future. For too long, due to the number of zones and other factors, the City's commercial and mixed-use zones have been confusing and inconsistent—27 separate zoning districts that create red tape, limit housing options, and make it harder to build the kinds of places residents say they want. This proposal streamlines those districts into just six new mixed-use (MU) zones, making the rules easier to understand and use while still protecting neighborhood character and quality of life. The new MU zones will support vibrant, walkable neighborhoods with a mix of housing, jobs, and local businesses: especially near frequent transit lines. They ensure thoughtful design through improved standards for open space, landscaping, and transitions to adjacent homes. And they expand the kinds of housing types allowed citywide, including cottages, row houses, and small multifamily buildings, helping meet the needs of residents across incomes and life stages. We appreciate the City's robust outreach process, including walking tours, open houses, and multiple Planning Commission briefings. This level of community engagement has helped shape a well-balanced proposal that reflects public input and promotes the long-term health of Salt Lake City's neighborhoods. We urge you to adopt the Mixed-Use Zoning Consolidation and continue Salt Lake City's leadership in smart, inclusive land use planning. Thank you for your dedication to building a city where everyone can thrive. Sincerely, Turner C. Bitton (he/him) Executive Director SLC Neighbors for More Neighbors
